title.raw: Deep Lacerations: Do I Need Stitches or Glue?
title.rendered: Deep Lacerations: Do I Need Stitches or Glue?

content.raw:
We’ve all been there: a slip of the kitchen knife, a tumble on the pavement, or a DIY project gone wrong. In those first few seconds after a deep cut, your mind starts racing. Is it deep? Does it need a doctor? Should I just use a bandage and hope for the best? Deciding whether you need Professional medical attention for a wound is more than just about stopping the bleeding. It’s about preventing infection, ensuring the wound heals with minimal scarring, and making sure no underlying nerves or tendons are damaged. If you are searching for stitches in Irving, TX, you likely need a quick, clear answer so you can take action. This guide will walk you through how to assess a laceration, what the treatment options look like, and how to stay safe on your way to the ER.

How to Tell if Your Cut Needs Professional Care

Not every scrape requires a trip to the emergency room or urgent care, but deep lacerations are different. According to MedlinePlus, a wound generally needs professional closure if it meets certain criteria.

The Depth and Length Rule

If a cut is deeper than a quarter-inch, you can see "yellow fat," or if the wound is gaping so wide that you cannot easily pull the edges together with gentle pressure, you likely need stitches. Any wound longer than half an inch often requires medical intervention to heal properly.

Persistent Bleeding

If you apply direct pressure to a wound for 10 to 15 minutes and it is still bleeding actively, this is a medical emergency. High-pressure "spurting" blood indicates an arterial injury, which requires immediate care at an ER.

Location Matters

The location of the cut significantly changes the treatment plan.
  • The Face: Cuts on the face are often treated with extra care to minimize scarring.
  • Joints: Lacerations over knuckles, elbows, or knees are difficult to keep closed with simple bandages because the skin stretches every time you move.
  • Hands and Feet: ASSH states that because we use our hands for almost everything, deep cuts here carry a higher risk of nerve or tendon damage.

Stitches vs. Medical Glue: What’s the Difference?

When you arrive at the ER for stitches in Irving, TX, the provider will evaluate whether "traditional" sutures or modern medical adhesives are best for your specific injury.

When Doctors Choose Traditional Sutures (Stitches)

Stitches (sutures) are the "gold standard" for deep or complex wounds. They are made of sterile thread-like material that manually holds the skin edges together.
  • Best for: Deep cuts, wounds over joints, or jagged lacerations.
  • Pros: They are incredibly strong and can hold high-tension areas together while they heal.
  • Cons: They require a follow-up visit for removal (unless they are the "absorbable" kind) and can be slightly more intimidating for children.

The Benefits of Medical Adhesive (Skin Glue)

Medical glue, often called "dermabond," is a specialized liquid adhesive. According to the FDA, these adhesives are designed to slough off naturally as the wound heals.
  • Best for: Small, straight cuts in areas with low tension (like the forehead or shins).
  • Pros: No needles are required, the process is very fast, and there is no need for a return visit to have them removed.
  • Cons: Glue cannot be used on joints, hairy areas, or wounds that are heavily bleeding or contaminated.

How long can you wait to get stitches?

Timing is everything when it comes to wound care. You should generally seek medical attention within 6 to 12 hours of the injury. Waiting too long increases the risk of infection significantly. Once a wound has been open for several hours, bacteria begin to colonize the area. If you wait more than 24 hours, many doctors will refuse to "stitch the wound shut" because doing so could trap bacteria inside, leading to a serious abscess or systemic infection. Early closure leads to better cosmetic results and faster return to normal activity. If you are unsure, it is always better to be evaluated sooner rather than later.

Caring for the wound on the way to the ER or Urgent Care

The steps you take in the first 20 minutes after an injury can make a huge difference in your recovery. Here is how to handle a deep laceration while you are en route to get stitches, Irving, TX:
  1. Apply Direct Pressure: Use a clean cloth or sterile gauze. Hold firm, steady pressure directly over the site for at least 10 minutes without "peeking" to see if it stopped.
  2. Elevate: If the injury is on an arm or leg, keep it raised above the level of your heart to slow the blood flow.
  3. Clean Gently (If Possible): If there is visible dirt, you can rinse the wound with cool water. NIH recommends not scrubbing the wound or using harsh chemicals like hydrogen peroxide or iodine, as these can actually damage the healthy tissue and slow down healing.
  4. Cover: Once bleeding is controlled, wrap the area in a clean bandage. Do not apply antibiotic ointments until a doctor has seen the wound, as it can interfere with medical glue if that ends up being the chosen treatment.

Tetanus shot updates: Why they matter for deep cuts

Whenever the skin is broken, especially by a dirty object, metal, or an animal bite, doctors worry about tetanus. Tetanus is a serious disease caused by bacteria found in soil, dust, and manure that enter the body through breaks in the skin. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get a tetanus booster (Td or Tdap) every 10 years. However, for a "dirty" or deep wound, a doctor may recommend a booster if your last shot was more than 5 years ago. Staying up to date on your vaccines is one of the simplest ways to prevent a life-threatening complication from a simple accident.

What to Expect During Your Visit

When you visit an urgent care or ER for a laceration, the process is usually straightforward:
  • Numbing: For stitches, the doctor will likely use a local anesthetic (like Lidocaine) to numb the area so you don’t feel a thing.
  • Irrigation: The wound will be thoroughly washed with sterile saline to remove any hidden debris.
  • Closure: The provider will use sutures, staples, or glue to close the skin.
  • Aftercare Instructions: You’ll receive specific instructions on how to keep the wound dry and when to return for a check-up.

Need Immediate Care for a Deep Cut in Irving, TX?

When accidents happen, waiting isn't an option. Whether you are dealing with persistent bleeding, a wound over a joint, or you are unsure whether you need stitches or medical glue, the ER of Irving is here to help. A deep cut closed within 6 to 12 hours has a lower risk of infection and scarring, and any wound that spurts blood or will not stop bleeding after 10 to 15 minutes of pressure needs emergency care now. See the emergency services at ER of Irving. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (972) 893-3148 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Does it hurt to get stitches?

The injury itself is usually the most painful part. Before placing stitches, providers use a very small needle to numb the area.

Can I use super glue from the store on a cut?

No. Household super glue contains chemicals that can irritate skin tissue and cause chemical burns. Medical-grade glue is sterile and specifically formulated to be flexible and safe for human tissue.

How do I know if my cut is infected?

Signs of infection include increasing pain, swelling, warmth around the wound, red streaks leading away from the cut, or pus-like drainage. If you have a fever, seek medical help immediately.

How long do stitches stay in?

It depends on the location. Stitches on the face may come out in 3–5 days to prevent scarring, while stitches on the joints or feet may need to stay in for 10–14 days.

Can I get my stitches wet?

Usually, you must keep the area dry for the first 24 to 48 hours. After that, your doctor may allow gentle washing with soap and water, but you should avoid soaking in a tub or pool until the stitches are removed.

Will I have a scar?

All deep cuts result in some level of scarring, but getting professional closure (stitches or glue) significantly reduces the size and visibility of the scar compared to letting the wound heal "open."

title.raw: High Fevers in Children: The 103° Rule
title.rendered: High Fevers in Children: The 103° Rule

content.raw:
The moment you see that digital thermometer climb to 103°F, your heart skips a beat. As a parent or caregiver, your instinct is to protect, and seeing your child flushed, shivering, or lethargic can be incredibly frightening. In the world of pediatrics, "103" is often cited as a critical milestone, but it is important to remember that a fever is not an illness itself; it is actually a sign that your child’s immune system is working exactly as it should to fight off an infection. However, knowing when that fever crosses the line from a "healthy defense" to a "medical priority" is vital for your peace of mind and your child's safety. This guide will walk you through the "103° Rule," how to manage symptoms at home, and exactly when it’s time to seek professional care.

Understanding the 103° Rule: Why Fever Height Matters

According to MedlinePlus, in medical terms, a fever is generally defined as a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. While a lower-grade fever might just mean a common cold, hitting the 103°F mark often signals a more robust inflammatory response.

The Body’s Natural Defense Mechanism

A fever is your child’s "internal thermostat" turning up the heat to make the body less hospitable to viruses and bacteria. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), most fevers are harmless and actually help the immune system.

Is 103°F Always an Emergency?

For an older child who is still drinking fluids and playing occasionally, a 103°F fever might be manageable at home with rest. However, the child's fever ER recommendation becomes much more urgent if the fever is persistent, doesn't respond to medicine, or is accompanied by "red flag" symptoms like a stiff neck or extreme irritability.

When to Seek Immediate Help: Child Fever ER Guidelines

Timing is everything. Depending on your child's age, a high temperature carries different levels of risk.

Age-Specific Fever Thresholds

  • Infants under 3 months: Medline states that any fever of 100.4°F or higher is considered a medical emergency. Newborns do not have fully developed immune systems, and a fever could indicate a serious bacterial infection.
  • 3 months to 3 years: A fever of 102.2°F or higher warrants a call to your pediatrician.
  • Any age: If the fever reaches 104°F or higher repeatedly, you should head to a Child fever ER immediately.

Beyond the Number: Looking at Behavior

Doctors often say, "Treat the child, not the thermometer." You should seek emergency care regardless of the number of symptoms if your child:
  • Is inconsolable or crying incessantly.
  • Has difficulty breathing or is wheezing.
  • Shows a purple or red spotted rash that doesn't fade when pressed.
  • Has a "bulging" soft spot (fontanelle) on their head.

Dehydration Signs: What to Watch For

High fevers lead to sweating and faster breathing, which can quickly deplete a child’s fluid levels. Preventing dehydration is one of the most important parts of fever management. According to MedlinePlus, you should monitor for these dehydration signs:
  1. Dry mouth and tongue: Look for "sticky" saliva or a parched look.
  2. Fewer wet diapers: No urination for more than 8–12 hours.
  3. No tears: Crying without any moisture in the eyes.
  4. Sunken eyes or soft spot: A physical dip in the eyes or the top of the head.
  5. Lethargy: Extreme sleepiness or difficulty waking up.
If your child cannot keep fluids down due to vomiting and has a high fever, a Child fever ER visit is necessary to administer IV fluids.

When a Fever Causes Seizures (Febrile Seizures)

Perhaps the most terrifying experience for a parent is witnessing a febrile seizure. These are convulsions triggered by a rapid spike in body temperature. While they look scary, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) notes that most febrile seizures are brief and do not cause brain damage. They typically occur in children between 6 months and 5 years old.

What to Do During a Seizure

  • Stay calm: Most seizures end within a minute or two.
  • Keep them safe: Place them on their side on a protected surface (like the floor) to prevent choking.
  • Do not restrain them: Do not try to stop the movements or put anything in their mouth.
  • Time it: If the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, call 911 immediately.
Any child experiencing their first febrile seizure should be evaluated in a Child fever ER to rule out other causes like meningitis.

At-Home Comfort Measures vs. Medical Intervention

If your child is over 3 months old and the fever is hovering around 101°F–102°F, you can focus on comfort:
  • Fluids: Offer water, Pedialyte, or popsicles frequently.
  • Light Clothing: Don't bundle them up; this traps heat.
  • Medication: Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed by your doctor. Never give aspirin to a child, as it is linked to Reye’s Syndrome, a rare but serious condition.
If these measures don't bring the temperature down or if your child's condition worsens, it's time to seek professional help.

What Pediatric-Friendly Emergency Care Looks Like

When your child is sick, the care environment matters. Emergency care for children works best when the team is set up to treat smaller bodies and to keep a frightened child calm. Helpful features of pediatric-ready emergency care include:
  • Appropriately sized equipment: smaller blood pressure cuffs, needles, and masks suited to children.
  • Weight-based dosing: medication doses calculated for a child’s size rather than an adult’s.
  • A calmer setting: private rooms and a quieter space that help reduce a child’s anxiety.
Knowing what to look for helps you choose the right place to bring your child in an emergency.

We Are Here for Your Family

If your child has a high fever and you’re feeling unsure, don't wait. The ER of Irving team provides expert care in a calm, pediatric-friendly ER environment. Seek emergency care for any fever in a baby under 3 months, a fever of 104°F or higher, a stiff neck, trouble breathing, a non-fading rash, a seizure, or signs of dehydration. See emergency high-fever care at ER of Irving. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (972) 893-3148 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Is a 103°F fever dangerous for a toddler? 

A 103°F fever itself isn't necessarily dangerous, but it requires close monitoring. If the fever lasts more than 24 hours or is accompanied by pain, earache, or cough, consult a professional.

Can I give my child a cold bath to break a fever? 

No. Cold water can cause shivering, which actually raises the internal body temperature. Use lukewarm water for a sponge bath instead.

How often should I check my child's temperature? 

There is no need to wake a sleeping child just to check their temperature unless your doctor specifically advises it. Rest is often more beneficial.

When should I take my child to the ER for a fever? 

Seek a Child fever ER if the temperature hits 104°F, if they have a seizure, show signs of dehydration, have trouble breathing, or are under 3 months old with any fever.

Why won't the fever go down after Tylenol? 

Fever medication typically drops a temperature by 1 to 2 degrees; it may not bring it back to "normal" (98.6°F). If it doesn't budge at all, contact your provider.

What are the most common "red flags" with a fever? 

A stiff neck, a new rash, extreme lethargy, or blue-tinted lips/nails are immediate signs that you need emergency medical intervention.

title.raw: Is it a Stroke? The Critical F.A.S.T. Guide for DFW Residents
title.rendered: Is it a Stroke? The Critical F.A.S.T. Guide for DFW Residents

content.raw:
A stroke is one of the most time-sensitive emergencies in medicine. Recognizing it within minutes, not hours, can be the difference between full recovery and lasting brain injury. The F.A.S.T. method makes recognition simple enough for anyone to use. This guide covers what a stroke is, how to spot one, what to do in the first 5 minutes, and what happens when you arrive at the ER of Irving.

What is a Stroke? Why Every Minute Counts

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of your brain stops. The brain tissue without blood begins dying within minutes, and the damage spreads fast. Roughly 1.9 million brain cells die every minute during a stroke, according to the American Stroke Association. That is why doctors say "time is brain." The earlier someone gets to an ER, the more brain tissue can be saved. Strokes come in two main forms. An ischemic stroke is caused by a clot blocking a brain artery. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a brain artery bursting. Both are emergencies, but they need different treatments at the ER.

The F.A.S.T. Method: 4 Warning Signs of Stroke

The CDC and the American Stroke Association both promote F.A.S.T. as the fastest way to recognize a stroke. Each letter points to one thing to check.

  • A – Arm weakness. Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward or feel heavy?
  • S – Speech difficulty. Ask them to repeat a simple sentence like "the sky is blue." Are the words slurred or jumbled?
  • T – Time to call 911. Even if symptoms seem to fade, call. Note the exact time symptoms started.

F.A.S.T. catches most strokes, but not all. The American Stroke Association warns about signs that are easy to dismiss. Vision loss in one eye, sudden severe dizziness, or trouble walking should not be brushed off. Posterior strokes affect the back of the brain. They often cause balance and vision problems instead of the classic face droop. Silent strokes show up on a CT scan with no obvious symptoms at the time. If something is sudden and severe, call 911. Even atypical strokes need the same urgent ER pathway.

The two types of stroke need opposite treatments. That is why the ER team moves fast to identify which one is happening. About 87% of strokes are ischemic, per MedlinePlus. A blood clot blocks an artery in the brain. If the patient arrives within 3 to 4.5 hours of symptom onset, doctors can use a clot-dissolving drug called tPA to restore blood flow. These patients need blood pressure control, sometimes surgery, and intensive care. A CT scan within the first hour at the ER is what tells the team which type they are dealing with.

The First 5 Minutes: Exactly What To Do

What you do in the first 5 minutes matters more than almost anything else.
  1. Call 911 immediately. Do not call a friend or search online. Just dial.
  2. Note the exact time symptoms started. Or the last time the person was definitely normal. This number decides whether tPA is on the table.
  3. Stay with them. Help them sit or lie down safely. Loosen tight clothing.
  4. Track any changes. Symptoms can worsen quickly. Tell the paramedics what changed.
  5. Do not give food, water, or medicine. Swallowing may be impaired. Anything by mouth can choke them.
Ambulances also notify the ER en route, so the stroke team is ready when you arrive.

These four mistakes happen often and waste the only thing that matters: time.

  • Don't give aspirin. Aspirin makes hemorrhagic strokes worse. The ER decides after the CT scan.
  • Don't wait to see if it passes. Symptoms that fade can be a TIA, or mini-stroke. About 1 in 3 TIA patients have a full stroke within a year.
  • Don't let them sleep it off. Stroke symptoms during sleep are how the time window gets missed. If you can't say when symptoms started, tPA usually isn't possible.

Most strokes are preventable. The CDC lists the major risk factors, and most are within your control. High blood pressure is the single biggest risk factor. Controlling it cuts stroke risk roughly in half. Diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, smoking, and obesity each raise the odds on their own. Texas-specific concerns add up too:
  • Summer heat. Dehydration thickens blood and can trigger ischemic strokes in vulnerable adults. Drink water on hot days.
  • Sleep apnea. Common and underdiagnosed in DFW. Untreated sleep apnea doubles stroke risk.
  • Age over 55. Risk doubles every decade after.
What helps: regular blood pressure checks, taking prescribed medications consistently, 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days, and not smoking. Atrial fibrillation needs aggressive management because it raises stroke risk fivefold.

At the ER of Irving, the stroke pathway starts the moment paramedics call ahead. Per NINDS stroke care guidelines, the goal is to compress every minute that matters:
  • First 15 minutes. Vital signs, blood draw, neurological exam by an ER physician.
  • Within 25 minutes. CT scan of the head to rule in or rule out bleeding.
  • Within 45 minutes. CT results read, neurologist consulted.
  • Within 60 minutes. Decision on tPA for ischemic strokes, or transfer to a comprehensive stroke center if needed.
Our 24/7 ER team is set up to keep the tPA window open. We coordinate with regional comprehensive stroke centers for cases that need endovascular thrombectomy or neurosurgery. If you suspect a stroke, call 911 and tell them to bring the patient here.

FAQs

How long after symptoms start is tPA still effective?

Up to 4.5 hours from symptom onset for most patients. Some select cases extend further. After that window, the risk of brain bleeding from tPA outweighs the benefit. Mechanical thrombectomy can extend the treatment window to 24 hours in some patients.

Can young people have strokes?

Yes. About 10 to 15% of strokes happen in adults under 50. Causes include heart conditions, blood clotting disorders, drug use, and head trauma. Sudden severe headache or vision loss in a young adult should not be dismissed.

What does a mini-stroke feel like?

A transient ischemic attack, or TIA, produces stroke-like symptoms that resolve within 24 hours, usually within an hour. The brain isn't permanently damaged, but a TIA is a strong warning sign. About 1 in 3 TIA patients have a full stroke within a year. Get evaluated.

Can stress trigger a stroke?

Chronic stress raises blood pressure and inflammation, both of which raise stroke risk. Acute emotional stress can trigger strokes in already-vulnerable adults, but it is rarely the sole cause.

What is the difference between a heart attack and a stroke?

A heart attack is a blockage in a heart artery, usually causing chest pain. A stroke is a blockage or bleed in a brain artery, causing neurological symptoms like face droop or speech trouble. Both need 911.

What is the recovery time after a stroke?

It varies. Many patients see meaningful recovery in 3 to 6 months with rehabilitation. Some have permanent deficits. The faster the initial treatment, the better the outcomes.

title.raw: Sudden Vision Loss or Eye Pain: Don't Wait
title.rendered: Sudden Vision Loss or Eye Pain: Don’t Wait

content.raw:
When it comes to our health, we often try to "tough it out." We might wait a few days to see if the cough clears up or if the sore muscle stops aching. However, your eyes are different. Vision is one of our most precious senses, and because the structures of the eye are so delicate, time is often the most critical factor in preventing permanent damage. If you are experiencing sudden eye pain or a change in your vision, it is your body’s way of sounding an alarm. Whether it’s an eye injury, ER visit, or a trip to an urgent care clinic, getting professional help immediately can be the difference between a full recovery and lifelong vision loss.

Recognizing the Red Flags: When to Seek Urgent Care

Not every eye issue requires a trip to the emergency room, but certain symptoms are universal "red flags." According to MedlinePlus, you should seek immediate medical attention if you experience:
  • Sudden, severe eye pain.
  • Pain accompanied by a headache, fever, or nausea.
  • A sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes.
  • Seeing halos around lights.
  • Physical trauma or a blow to the eye.

Chemical Splashes in the Eye

A chemical burn is one of the most time-sensitive emergencies you can face. Whether it’s a household cleaning agent, a garden chemical, or an industrial solvent, chemicals can cause deep tissue damage within seconds. If a chemical splashes in your eye, the National Institutes of Health (NEI) recommends immediate irrigation. You should flush your eye with clean, lukewarm water or saline solution for at least 15 minutes without stopping. While you are flushing, have someone else call 911 or prepare to take you to an eye injury ER. Do not wait to see if the stinging stops; some alkaline chemicals (like drain cleaners) can continue to damage the eye even after the initial pain subsides.

Scratched Cornea Symptoms: More Than Just an Irritation

The cornea is the clear, protective outer layer of your eye. According to AOA, because it is packed with nerve endings, even a tiny scratch, known as a corneal abrasion, can feel incredibly painful.

Common Signs of a Corneal Abrasion

According to the NIH, symptoms of a scratched cornea include:
  • A feeling like there is sand or grit in your eye.
  • Significant tearing and redness.
  • Sensitivity to light (photophobia).
  • Blurred vision.

Why You Shouldn't "Rub It Out"

It is an instinct to rub your eye when it feels irritated. However, if a foreign object like a piece of metal, glass, or even a grain of sand is present, rubbing can press the object deeper into the cornea, causing more severe damage or a potential infection called a corneal ulcer. If you suspect an eye injury ER visit is necessary. Keep the eye closed or loosely covered with a paper cup until a doctor can examine it.

When "Seeing Spots" is a Retinal Emergency

Most of us have seen the occasional "floater," those specks that drift across our field of vision. Usually, these are harmless. However, a sudden onset of new floaters can signal a retinal detachment. The National Eye Institute (NEI) notes that a retinal detachment occurs when the thin layer of tissue at the back of the eye pulls away from its normal position. This is a painless but sight-threatening emergency. Watch for these symptoms:
  1. Flashers: Seeing sudden streaks of light or "lightning bolts."
  2. A "Curtain" Effect: A dark shadow or curtain moving across your field of vision from the side, top, or bottom.
  3. Shower of Floaters: A sudden, massive increase in the number of spots you see.
If you experience these, you need an immediate evaluation by an ophthalmologist or an emergency department to prevent permanent blindness in that eye.

Sudden Vision Loss: Understanding the Risks

Losing your vision suddenly, even if it returns after a few minutes, is never normal. It can be a sign of an "eye stroke" (clogged blood vessels in the retina) or even a precursor to a systemic stroke. The NIH emphasizes that sudden vision changes are one of the key warning signs of a stroke. When blood flow to the eye or the brain is interrupted, every second counts. If you experience a sudden "blackout" in your vision, treat it with the same urgency as chest pain.

Protecting Your Sight: Immediate Steps to Take

If you or a loved one experiences an eye emergency, follow these steps while heading to the ER:
  • Do not apply pressure to the eyeball.
  • Do not attempt to remove a foreign object that appears embedded in the eye.
  • Do not apply any ointments or over-the-counter drops unless instructed by a professional.
  • Do stay calm and keep both eyes as still as possible to prevent further irritation.

Don't Wait, Protect Your Vision!

If you're experiencing sudden vision loss or eye pain, seek immediate care at the ER of Irving. Our team is ready to evaluate and treat eye emergencies 24/7. Need immediate help? Visit the ER of Irving for fast, expert treatment of sudden vision loss and eye injuries. Call us now at (972) 893-3148 for immediate assistance or to speak with a healthcare professional. Stay informed with helpful tips on recognizing eye emergencies and keeping your family safe. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for health updates.

FAQs

How do I know if I should go to the ER for an eye injury? 

You should go to an eye injury ER if you have sudden vision loss, a penetrating injury (something stuck in the eye), a chemical splash, or severe pain that doesn't go away.

Can a scratched cornea heal on its own? 

While minor scratches may heal, they often require antibiotic drops to prevent infection. 

What causes sudden flashes of light in my eyes? 

Flashes are often caused by the vitreous gel inside your eye pulling on the retina. 

What should I do if I get soap or cleaning chemicals in my eye? 

Immediately flush the eye with water for 15 minutes and seek medical advice. 

Is a red eye always an emergency? 

Not always. Redness from "pink eye" (conjunctivitis) or allergies is common. However, if the redness is accompanied by deep pain, light sensitivity, or vision changes, it requires an urgent evaluation.

Can I drive myself to the doctor if I have an eye injury? 

No. If your vision is impaired or you are in pain, you should have someone else drive you or call emergency services. Driving with compromised vision is dangerous for you and others.
